Introduction
to Python
By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
•
Identify and use common Python datatypes,
including strings, integers, floats, and
Booleans.
•
Create, access, and change variables to store
information in a program.
•
Use print() to display values in the console.
•
Use clear and descriptive names when
creating variables.

print()
Displaying Output with
print("Hello World")
The print() function displays
information in the console.
Anything inside quotation marks
is treated as text.
OUTPUT
Hello World

Variables
score = 100
A variable is a named location
that stores a value.
name = "Alex"
Variables allow programs to
remember information and use
print(score)
it later.
print(name)
Think of a variable as a labeled
container: the variable name is
the label, and the value is what
OUTPUT
is stored inside. 100
Alex

Variables vs. Literals
age = 15
A literal is a value written
directly in your code.
print(age) # Variable
A variable stores a value under
print(15) # Literal
a name.
Both display 15, but the variable
can be reused or changed later.
OUTPUT
15
15

Datatypes
name = "Alex" # str
A datatype describes what kind
of information a value contains. age = 15 # int
height = 1.72 # float
The datatype determines how
is_student = True # bool
Python can use the value.
To the right are the most
common primitive datatypes.

str
Strings ( )
name = "Alex"
A string stores text as a
sequence of characters. message = "Hello World"
number = "42"
Strings must be surrounded by
quotation marks.
Numbers surrounded by
quotation marks are also
treated as strings rather than
numbers.

Numbers
students = 24 # int
Python commonly uses two
datatypes for numbers. temp = 21.5 # float
An int stores a whole number,
while a float stores a number
with a decimal value.
Python determines which
datatype to use based on the
value being stored.

int
Integers ( )
age = 16
An integer is a whole number
without a decimal point. score = 100
temperature = -5
Integers can be positive,
negative, or zero.
They are useful for values that
are counted using whole
numbers.

float
Floats ( )
price = 9.99
A float is a number that
contains a decimal point. height = 1.72
temperature = -3.5
Floats are useful for
measurements and other
values that may contain a
fractional or decimal amount.

bool
Booleans ( )
is_student = True
A Boolean stores one of two
possible values: True or False. game_over = False
Booleans are commonly used to
represent whether a condition is
currently true or false.
In Python, True and False must
begin with capital letters.

Initializing Variables
score = 100
Initializing a variable means
creating it and assigning its first player_name = "Alex"
value.
Python uses the equals sign (=)
to assign a value to a variable.
The variable name goes on the
left of =, and the value being
stored goes on the right.

Naming Variables
player_score = 100
Variable names should clearly
describe the information they student_name = "Alex"
store. number_of_lives = 3
Python variables should
normally use snake_case, with
lowercase words separated by
underscores.
Use descriptive words instead of
unclear abbreviations or single-
letter names.

Accessing Variables
score = 100
Accessing a variable means
using the value currently stored
inside it. print(score)
Use the variable's name
whenever you want to access
its value.
OUTPUT
100

Changing Variables
score = 100
A variable can be changed by
assigning a new value to it. print(score)
The new value replaces the
score = 90
value that was previously
stored. print(score)
OUTPUT
100
90

Putting It Together
player_name = "Alex"
Variables allow programs to
store information, access that score = 100
information later, and change it game_over = False
as the program runs.
Each variable has a name, print(player_name)
stores a value, and has a print(score)
datatype based on the value
being stored.
score = 150
print(score)

Congratulations!
You have completed the introduction to
Python!
You should now be able to create
variables using appropriate datatypes,
access and change their values, and
display information using print().
